title: Weaving in ends — securing yarn tails without a knot
subtitle: Duplicate the path of existing stitches with the tail to lock it without knots
excerpt: Weaving in a crochet yarn tail means threading it through the bodies of surrounding stitches in a pattern that locks it under tension — not a knot. The tail should travel in at least two different directions through the stitches to prevent it pulling through. Done correctly, the tail is invisible and permanent.

glossaryTerms.definition: Finishing technique where yarn tails are secured by threading them through the bodies of surrounding stitches with a tapestry needle. The tail travels in at least two directions through the fabric — typically forward along the stitch, then back — to prevent pull-through.

heroPrompt: A tapestry needle threading a cream yarn tail through the back of a crochet fabric in a zigzag path, close-up showing the needle entering and exiting stitch bodies.

content.text: is the last step of any crochet project and the one most often done badly — too short, only in one direction, or knotted. Knots loosen and show through the fabric over time. A properly woven tail uses the friction of the stitch structure to hold the tail permanently without any knot.
Weaving in on the wrong side
Thread the tail onto a tapestry needle. Work on the wrong side of the piece.
Pass the needle through the back bar or the body of 4-5 adjacent stitches in one direction — for example, along the row horizontally.
Change direction: turn 90 degrees or reverse and pass the needle through 4-5 more stitch bodies. The tail now crosses its own path.
Trim the remaining tail close to the fabric — about 2-3 mm. The woven portion holds without a knot.

items.symptom: Tail works its way out during wear or washing
items.cause: Woven only in one direction, or not long enough
items.fix: The tail must travel in at least two different directions through the fabric body. The minimum woven length is about 5 cm — shorter tails will pull free, especially in smooth or slippery yarns.

items.symptom: Tail shows on the right side
items.cause: Needle passing through the stitch and out the right-side surface
items.fix: Work on the wrong side only. Insert the needle through stitch bodies sideways — through the stitch body itself, not through the open space between stitches.

content.text: For slippery yarns (silk, bamboo, linen), split the tail into individual plies and weave each ply separately in different directions — the separated plies grip the fabric better than the full strand. For superwash wool, a small knot is acceptable since superwash yarn is particularly slippery and single-direction weaving can fail.
